slides: Semantic precision.
It's one of the places where students lose the most points in language... and the easiest one to protect yourself from.
Let's start with some definitions.
Semantics is the part of linguistics that deals with the link between words and what they mean.
When NITE talks about semantic precision, it means using words in a way that matches their meaning exactly.
One, using a word or expression correctly... but in a place where it doesn't fit. So it means something different from what we wanted to say.
Two, twisting the expression or the word. We take a word or an expression, and write it in a different, wrong form.
So those are the two problems that make up imprecision.
Using a word or expression in a way that isn't precise, or out of context, may hurt your score.
Now, why do I say 'may', and not 'lowers the score'? Because it really depends.
Again, NITE understands that we write the essay in thirty-five minutes, and it's a draft.
If there's a mistake or two here and there, even a language mistake, or a word that isn't precise, we probably won't lose points for it.
But if it happens several times, they'll take points off.
And by the way, semantic imprecision is one of the places where students lose the most points. It's one of the most common mistakes.
And the reason is that students try to impress the rater.
In language, I want to impress the rater. I want him to think my language is richer than it really is.
Now look, there's a difference here between content and language.
In content, I have my level. I have critical thinking, I build arguments in a certain way.
And I try to reach a bit higher, because I always want a little more than I can do. So I add another piece of support, something like that.
If it works, great. If it doesn't... nothing happened. My support, my sentences, my arguments, the link to the task, it's all still there.
In language, it's not like that. I'm at a certain level, and I try to impress the rater. I try to reach higher.
As long as it works, fine. Nice, I raised my language score a little.
But if it doesn't work, I don't stay where I was. My score gets hurt. I lose points.
Think about it like this. Forget the rater for a moment. Let's go to real life.
Sometimes we want to impress our friends. So how do I try to impress them? I do some trick I'm really good at.
I don't know... come see me lift the front wheel. Hop, I do a wheelie. Nice.
As long as I really know how to do the trick, or really know how to do a wheelie, great. I impressed them.
But if I don't know how... I start the trick, and suddenly they see me slipping the card in. Or I lift the wheel, and crash.
Now I'm worse off than before. Not only didn't I impress them... now they're laughing at me.
It's the same in the exam, in the essay. When you use a word or expression the wrong way, that's semantic imprecision, and you lose points. You make things worse for yourself.
So I really, really want to stress this, and ask you. Don't use words you're not a hundred percent sure of.
The ones where you think, 'hop, now I'll use this, and the rater will fall off his chair'. If you're not completely sure, drop it. Let it go.
Now let's look at sentences from students' essays. Students who tried to write 'high'. And let's see how to fix them, without showing off, and without taking risks you don't need.
First example.
'Free reign'. That's not the expression. The expression is 'free rein'. Like the reins of a horse, let loose.
So even though the rater probably understands what the student meant, they'll probably take points off here. It isn't the right expression.
So here we have a twisted expression.
And honestly, the simplest fix is to not need the idiom at all. Just say it plainly.
The word 'elitists' doesn't fit here.
An elitist is a person who believes a small, superior group should lead. The student meant the powerful groups themselves.
So, not focus only on the elites... or only on the stronger groups.
So here too there's a wrong word. They meant to write 'elites', and they wrote 'elitists'. So it's used incorrectly.
'Administrative-wise'? That's someone making up an expression. I don't really understand what he means... and the rater won't either.
And since there's no such expression, and we said we don't make up expressions, they take points off here.
Just say what you actually mean.
'Moral veto'. Again, a made-up expression. There's no such thing as a moral veto.
Now, the state simply has no right to harm the right of parents... But now 'right' shows up twice in the same sentence.
So we can say the state has no legitimate grounds for violating the parents' right. Again, here there was a made-up expression, one that doesn't exist.
Another made-up expression. What is 'sportive time'? What did he mean? Time meant for sport.
So write, time set aside for sport. Here too, it's a wrong expression. There's no such expression.
Now here we have the expression 'shoot themselves in the foot'. It's a real expression, and this time it's written correctly.
But it's used in a place that doesn't fit.
What does it mean to shoot yourself in the foot? You do something... and by mistake, you end up hurting yourself.
Here we're talking about people who publish private information about citizens without permission. They're not hurting themselves by mistake. They're hurting others, on purpose, from the start.
So even though the expression is correct, it's not in the right place. What it means doesn't fit the sentence.
And in this case, look. Instead of 'will shoot themselves in the foot and publish', just, will publish.
So simple. Instead of taking a risk... instead of trying to lift the wheel when I don't really know how to do a wheelie.
Here too, the word 'uniformity' is used wrong. What he wanted to say is 'unity'.
Now notice, this isn't a spelling mistake. He really meant to write 'uniformity', because he thought that was the meaning that fits.
But uniformity means everyone is the same. Unity means people are together. The word that fits here is 'unity'. So that's also semantic imprecision.
In English there are lots of pairs like this. Words that look or sound alike, but mean different things. Here are some that show up a lot in essays.
If you're not sure which one is which, use a different, simpler word that you are sure of.
Students are often told to change their words so they don't repeat themselves. But with the key term of the essay... that's a trap.
Face-recognition cameras, then security cameras, then surveillance. Regular security cameras don't recognize faces. So the rater wonders, did you change the topic?
So keep the key term. Change everything else around it. And 'these cameras' is fine. It clearly points back to the same thing.
Remember the 'moral veto' sentence? There, we avoided using the same word twice in one short sentence. That's style. But the key term of the essay stays the same.
So let's sum up the most important lesson here.
Don't use words and expressions if you're not a hundred percent sure what they mean, or how to write them correctly. Okay?
It's this thing where you try to impress... but in practice, you hurt your score.
And again, from checking tens of thousands of essays, this is one of the most common mistakes, and one of the main reasons students lose points in language.
Okay, that's it for semantic precision. Next, we're moving on to grammar. And as usual, I'll be waiting for you there.
